'''Alexander Theodore "Sasha" Shulgin''' (June 17, 1925 – June 2, 2014) was an [[American people|American]] [[biochemist]] who [[chemical synthesis|synthesized]] and tested over 200{{nbsp}}[[psychedelic drug|psychedelic]] and related [[chemical compound]]s.<ref name="Power2014">{{cite web | last=Power | first=Mike | title=Alexander Shulgin obituary | website=The Guardian | date=3 June 2014 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2014/jun/03/alexander-shulgin}}</ref><ref name="Bennett2005">{{cite news |first = Drake |last = Bennett |date = January 30, 2005 |title = Dr. Ecstasy |work = [[The New York Times Magazine]] | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2005/01/30/magazine/30ECSTASY.html |access-date = July 8, 2006 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111117063356/http://www.nytimes.com/2005/01/30/magazine/30ECSTASY.html| archive-date=November 17, 2011| url-status= live | quote = Shulgin tested for activity by taking the chemicals himself&nbsp;... Most of the scientific community considers Shulgin at best a curiosity and at worst a menace. Now, however, near the end of his career, his faith in the potential of psychedelics has at least a chance at vindication. A little more than a month ago, the Food and Drug Administration approved a Harvard Medical School study looking at whether MDMA can alleviate the fear and anxiety of terminal cancer patients. And next month will mark a year since Michael Mithoefer, a psychiatrist in Charleston, S.C., started his study of Ecstasy-assisted therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. }}</ref><ref name="Romero1995">{{cite news | first = Dennis | last = Romero | url = http://www.erowid.org/culture/characters/shulgin_alexander/shulgin_alexander_interview1.shtml | title = Sasha Shulgin, Psychedelic Chemist | newspaper = [[Los Angeles Times]] | date = September 5, 1995 | access-date = July 8, 2006 | archive-date = March 26, 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070326004128/http://www.erowid.org/culture/characters/shulgin_alexander/shulgin_alexander_interview1.shtml | url-status = live | quote = "I first explored mescaline in the late '50s," Shulgin says. "Three-hundred-fifty to 400 milligrams. I learned there was a great deal inside me," he replies.}}</ref> Among the most notable psychedelic and related drugs that Shulgin developed include [[2C-B]],<ref name="Nolan2019">{{cite web | last=Nolan | first=James | title=2C-B Is the Drug Taking Over the UK's Clubs | website=VICE | date=5 March 2019 | url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/what-is-2cb-and-its-effects/ | access-date=16 July 2026 | quote=First synthesised in 1974 by Alexander Shulgin – the man who famously popularised MDMA‘s use in psychology – 2C-B itself began as a therapeutic aid, [...]}}</ref><ref name="Ford2024">{{cite web | last=Ford | first=Celia | title=What in the world is pink cocaine? | website=Vox | date=4 November 2024 | url=https://www.vox.com/future-perfect/378046/pink-cocaine-tuci-2cb-drugs-liam-payne-peso-pluma | access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref> [[DOM (drug)|DOM]] (STP),<ref name="Lambert2014">{{cite web | last=Lambert | first=Molly | title=» Alexander Shulgin (1925-2014): Godfather of Psychedelics and Ecstacist | website= » Sports and Pop Culture from our rotating cast of writers – Grantland | date=4 June 2014 | url=https://grantland.com/hollywood-prospectus/alexander-shulgin-1925-2014-godfather-of-psychedelics-and-ecstacist/ | access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="TroutDaley2024">{{cite journal | vauthors = Trout K, Daley PF | title = The origin of 2,5-dimethoxy-4-methylamphetamine (DOM, STP) | journal = Drug Test Anal | volume = 16 | issue = 12 | pages = 1496–1508 | date = December 2024 | pmid = 38419183 | doi = 10.1002/dta.3667 | url = https://shulginresearch.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/The-origin-of-25-dimethoxy-4-methylamphetamine-DOM-STP.-Trout.-Drug-Test.-Anal.-DOI-10.1002-dta.3667-2024.pdf}}</ref><ref name="Baggott2023">{{cite journal | last=Baggott | first=Matthew J. | title=Learning about STP: A Forgotten Psychedelic from the Summer of Love | journal=History of Pharmacy and Pharmaceuticals | volume=65 | issue=1 | date=1 October 2023 | issn=2694-3034 | doi=10.3368/hopp.65.1.93 | pages=93–116 | url=https://hopp.uwpress.org/content/wphopp/65/1/93.full-text.pdf}}</ref> and [[Ariadne (drug)|Ariadne]] (4C-D; BL-3912; Dimoxamine).<ref name="CunninghamBockSerrano2023" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="ShulginManningDaley2011-Ariadne" /><ref name="Shulgin1987" /> In addition, he is known for discovering and describing the unique effects of the [[entactogen]] [[MDMA]] (ecstasy), which led to its use in [[MDMA-assisted psychotherapy]] and to its widespread use as a [[recreational drug]], for instance in the [[rave]] scene.<ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Romero1995" /><ref name="BenzenhöferPassie2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Benzenhöfer U, Passie T | title = Rediscovering MDMA (ecstasy): the role of the American chemist Alexander T. Shulgin | journal = Addiction | volume = 105 | issue = 8 | pages = 1355–1361 | date = August 2010 | pmid = 20653618 | doi = 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.02948.x | url = }}</ref>

Shulgin studied chemistry at [[Harvard University]] and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and received his Ph.D. in biochemistry in 1955.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Kent2014" /> He developed the best-selling [[biodegradable]] [[pesticide]] [[mexacarbate]] (Zectran) while working at [[Dow Chemical Company]] in the early 1960s.<ref name="Peplow2014" /><ref name="Power2014" /> Shulgin became interested in [[psychedelic chemistry]] after having his first [[psychedelic experience]] in 1960 and from then on began developing new psychedelic compounds in his lab at his home in [[Lafayette, California]].<ref name="Jay2019" /><ref name="Pollan2021">{{cite book | vauthors = Pollan M | author-link = Michael Pollan | section = Mescaline | pages = 161–248 | title = This Is Your Mind on Plants | date = 2021 | publisher = Penguin Press | location = New York | isbn = 978-0-593-29690-5 | section-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=Fxs3EAAAQBAJ&pg=PA161 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=Fxs3EAAAQBAJ}}</ref><ref name="PassieBrandt2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Passie T, Brandt SD | title = Self-Experiments with Psychoactive Substances: A Historical Perspective | journal = Handb Exp Pharmacol | volume = 252 | issue = | pages = 69–110 | date = 2018 | pmid = 30478735 | doi = 10.1007/164_2018_177 | url = }}</ref><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="Langlitz2012">{{cite book | last=Langlitz | first=Nicolas | chapter=Between Animality and Divinity | pages=166–203 | title=Neuropsychedelia: The Revival of Hallucinogen Research since the Decade of the Brain | publisher=University of California Press | date=7 November 2012 | isbn=978-0-520-27481-5 | doi=10.1525/california/9780520274815.003.0006 | url=http://california.universitypressscholarship.com/view/10.1525/california/9780520274815.001.0001/upso-9780520274815 | quote=They had invited [...] and Alexander “Sasha” Shulgin who, since quitting his job as a research chemist at Dole Chemical Company in 1966, had dedicated his life to developing new psychedelic drugs in a private lab on his farm in Lafayette, California.}}</ref> His approach was to synthesize the compounds, [[self-experimentation|test them on himself]] and a [[Shulgin research group|small group of trusted others]], and document his findings.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="PassieBrandt2018" /> He formally published on psychedelics in the [[scientific literature]] for decades, before publishing his books ''[[PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story]]'' (''Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved'') in 1991 and ''[[TiHKAL: The Continuation]]'' (''Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved'') in 1997.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="PassieBrandt2018" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="TiHKAL">{{CiteTiHKAL}}</ref> These books documented his and others' work with hundreds of [[substituted phenethylamine|phenethylamine]]s, [[substituted tryptamine|tryptamine]]s, and [[substituted lysergamide|lysergamide]]s, including their [[chemical synthesis|chemical syntheses]], properties and effects, and discussion.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="TiHKAL" /> They were coauthored by Shulgin and by his wife [[Ann Shulgin]], a pioneering [[psychedelic therapist]], whom he met in 1978 and married in 1981.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Risen2022">{{cite web | last=Risen | first=Clay | title=Ann Shulgin, 91, Who Explored Psychedelics With Her Husband, Dies | website=The New York Times | date=19 July 2022 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/19/science/ann-shulgin-dead.html | language=en-US | access-date=15 July 2026 | page=}}</ref><ref name="Warren2022">{{cite web | last=Warren | first=Penny | title=Ann Shulgin obituary | website=The Guardian | date=5 August 2022 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2022/aug/05/ann-shulgin-obituary | access-date=15 July 2026}}</ref> Shulgin was an [[academic staff|academic]] and taught at universities such as the University of California, Berkeley, the [[University of California, San Francisco]], and [[San Francisco State University]].<ref name="Hanna2014" /><ref name="Greendyk2021" />

Shulgin had a close and friendly relationship with the [[Drug Enforcement Administration]] (DEA) for many decades and held a DEA license to work with [[Controlled Substances Act#Schedule I|Schedule I]] [[controlled substance]]s.<ref name="Bennett2005" /> Following the publication of ''PiHKAL'' however, Shulgin's lab was raided by the DEA in 1993.<ref name="Bennett2005" /> He was stripped of his license and fined due to a violation of its terms.<ref name="Bennett2005" /> According to a DEA representative, "It is our opinion that those books are pretty much cookbooks on how to make illegal drugs."<ref name="Bennett2005" /> There have also been [[overdose]]s and [[death]]s due to compounds that Shulgin developed, which he has expressed frustration and sadness about, but also emphasized personal freedom and that all drugs have risks.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Platoni2002">{{cite web | last=Platoni | first=Kara | title=2C-T-7's Bad Trip | website=East Bay Express (EBX) | date=1 May 2002 | url=https://eastbayexpress.com/2c-t-7s-bad-trip-1/}}</ref><ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> During his life, Shulgin advocated for use of psychedelics and for legalization of all drugs.<ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Davidson1997">{{cite web | last=Davidson | first=Ros | title=Archive, 1997: Interview with Alexander Shulgin, 'godfather of ecstasy' | website=The Guardian | date=3 June 2014 | orig-date=1997 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/from-the-archive-blog/2014/jun/03/shulgin-alexander-drugs-ecstasy-mdma}}</ref> He has historically been a polarizing figure, seen variously as a "hero of the counterculture", "curiosity", and "menace".<ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Peplow2014">{{cite web | last=Peplow | first=Mark | title=A mind-blowing legacy | website=Chemistry World | date=11 June 2014 | url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/opinion/a-mind-blowing-legacy/7457.article | access-date=16 July 2026 | quote=For some, Alexander Shulgin was a bold explorer at the frontiers of neurochemistry. To others, he was the wanton architect of a wave of dangerous recreational drugs: the godfather of ecstasy. [...] Perhaps it is because pure motives are not always enough to absolve a chemist of responsibility when their work is misused. Or, as a hysterical Mail on Sunday headline screamed after a spate of ecstasy-related deaths in 2001: ‘Has Dr Shulgin killed 100 British teenagers?’}}</ref><ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Appendino G, Minassi A, Taglialatela-Scafati O | title = Recreational drug discovery: natural products as lead structures for the synthesis of smart drugs | journal = Natural Product Reports | volume = 31 | issue = 7 | pages = 880–904 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 24823967 | doi = 10.1039/c4np00010b | url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262304038 | access-date = September 3, 2019 | archive-date = September 28, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200928144853/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262304038_Recreational_drug_discovery_Natural_products_as_lead_structures_for_the_synthesis_of_smart_drugs | url-status = live | quote = While various artists and writers, including Sartre, experimented with mescaline at that time, by far the most far-reaching effects associated to this cultural climate and to the secularization of mescaline are those related to Alexander Shulgin. After experiencing with mescaline, Shulgin, a Berkeley graduate, developed an active interest in mind-altering drugs and the systematic study of their effect in humans. Shulgin claimed that mescaline made him aware of the existence of a world buried in our spirit, whose “availability” was “catalyzed” by chemicals. The consequences of these insights were devastating. [...]}}</ref>

Shulgin has been described as the "greatest [[psychedelic chemist]] of all time".<ref name="Kent2014">{{Cite web |last=Kent |first=James L. |date=September 10, 2014 |title=Godfather of Ecstasy: Alexander Shulgin's Last Trip |url=https://hightimes.com/culture/godfather-of-ecstasy-alexander-shulgins-last-trip/ |access-date=April 15, 2023 |website=[[High Times]] |language=en-US | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200311075358/https://hightimes.com/culture/godfather-of-ecstasy-alexander-shulgins-last-trip/ | archive-date = 2020-03-11 | url-status = dead | quote=When I ask Ann about his favorite among all the chemical compounds he’d created, she answers immediately: “It would have to be 2C-B. He was always very proud of that one. He called it the ‘Great Teacher’ … although I preferred 2C-B-FLY a bit more.” [...] Although Shulgin worked with many types of drugs, his favorites were the phenethylamines, psychedelics that are more thoughtful than overpowering.}}</ref><ref name="Morris2010">{{cite web | author = Hamilton Morris | title = The Last Interview With Alexander Shulgin: Which, Technically, Was Not an Interview at All | date = 2 May 2010 | publisher = [[Vice Media]] | website = vice.com | url = https://isomerdesign.com/bitnest/external/Vice/v17n5_us17 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201018023408/http://www.vice.com/en/article/avjewz/the-last-interview-with-alexander-shulgin-423-v17n5 | archive-date = 18 October 2020 | quote = Ask Shulgin what his favorite psychedelic is and he will say “2CB”5 without hesitation. ==Early life and education ==
Shulgin was born on June 17, 1925,<ref name="Kent2014" /> in [[Berkeley, California]],<ref name="Ancestry2005">Ancestry.com. California Birth Index, 1905–1995 [database on-line]. Provo, Utah: Ancestry.com Operations Inc, 2005. Original data: State of California. California Birth Index, 1905–1995. Sacramento, California: State of California Department of Health Services, Center for Health Statistics.</ref> to Theodore Stevens Shulgin (1893–1978)<ref name="Ancestry2000">Ancestry.com. California Death Index, 1940–1997 [database on-line]. Provo, Utah: Ancestry.com Operations Inc, 2000. Original data: State of California. California Death Index, 1940–1997. Sacramento, California: State of California Department of Health Services, Center for Health Statistics.</ref> and Henrietta D. (Aten) Shulgin (1894–1960).<ref name="Ancestry2000" /><ref>{{cite book|author =Lawrence, Alberta Chamberlain |title=Authors Biographical Monthly Service |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TEE7AQAAIAAJ |year=1952 |publisher=Golden Syndicate Publishing Company}}</ref> His father was born in [[Chelyabinsk]], [[Russia]] and was a refugee of the [[Russian Revolution]];<ref name="Margolin2022">{{cite web | last=Margolin | first=Madison | title=Inside the Chemistry Lab Where the MDMA Godfather Synthesized Novel Psychedelics | website=DoubleBlind Mag | date=11 July 2022 | url=https://doubleblindmag.com/inside-sasha-shulgins-lab/ | access-date=18 July 2026}}</ref> his mother was born in [[Illinois]]. Theodore and Henrietta were public school teachers in [[Alameda County]], [[California]].<ref>Ancestry.com. 1930 United States Federal Census [database on-line]. Provo, Utah: Ancestry.com Operations Inc, 2002. Year: 1930; Census Place: Berkeley, Alameda, California; Roll 111; Page: 1B; Enumeration District: 320; File: 1029.0.</ref>

Shulgin studied [[organic chemistry]] at [[Harvard University]] as a scholarship student, and was enrolled there at the age of 16.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Wolfson2014">{{cite journal | last=Wolfson | first=Philip | title=Alexander Theodore “Sasha” Shulgin 1925-2014 | journal=Herbalgram: The Journal of the American Botanical Council | issue = 104 | pages = 75–76 | date=2014 | url=https://www.herbalgram.org/resources/herbalgram/issues/104/table-of-contents/hg104-obit-shulgin/}}</ref><ref name="MAPS2014a" /> He dropped out to join the [[U.S. Navy]], during his second year at Harvard.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Wolfson2014" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /> In 1944, a [[military nurse]] gave Shulgin a glass of orange juice prior to a surgery for a thumb infection, while serving on [[USS Pope (DE-134)|USS ''Pope'']] during [[World War II|World War{{nbsp}}II]]; he drank the juice and, assuming that crystals at the bottom of the glass were a [[sedative]], "fell unconscious".<ref name="Bennett2005" />{{Additional citation needed|date=July 2026}} Upon waking he learned that the crystals were undissolved sugar, and that doctors had administered anesthesia after he was already unconscious—an experience Drake Bennett of ''[[The New York Times Magazine]]'' referred to as "revelatory", and a "tantalizing hint of the mind's odd strength", as "his collapse was caused entirely by the placebo effect".<ref name="Bennett2005" />{{Additional citation needed|date=July 2026}}

After serving in the armed forces, Shulgin returned to California, and earned his PhD in [[biochemistry]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="Power2014" /> Through the late 1950s, Shulgin completed [[post-doctoral]] work in the fields of [[psychiatry]] and pharmacology at [[University of California, San Francisco]]. 

==Career==
After working at [[Bio-Rad Laboratories]] as a research director for a brief period, Shulgin began his career at [[Dow Chemical Company]].<ref name="Power2014" />

Shulgin first heard of [[mescaline]] in the mid-1940s and read about it over the years, including the works of early researchers like [[:de:Kurt Beringer|Kurt Beringer]] and [[Alexandre Rouhier]] and the later works of [[Aldous Huxley]] among others.<ref name="Jay2019">{{cite book | last=Jay | first=Mike | title=Mescaline: A Global History of the First Psychedelic | publisher=Yale University Press | date=18 June 2019 | isbn=978-0-300-23107-6 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6IKVDwAAQBAJ | quote = The most consequential mescaline trip of the sixties was, with hindsight, the one taken in April 1960 by Alexander Shulgin, a biochemist at Dow Chemical Company in California who had recently completed his postdoctoral studies in pharmacology at Berkeley. He had read Huxley and followed his footsteps back to Beringer and Rouhier, and was surprised by how little pharmacological work had been done on mescaline’s wider chemical family. When a psychologist offered him the chance to try it, he accepted eagerly, and the experience ‘unquestionably confirmed the entire direction of my life’. He was awoken to colour and visual detail as never before, and continually struck with novel insights, but ‘more than anything else, the world amazed me, in that I saw it as I had when I was a child’. He found himself immersed in ‘a space wherein I had once roamed as an immortal explorer, and I was recalling everything that had been known authentically to me then, and which I had abandoned, then forgotten, with the coming of age’.52 He decided on the spot that if there were similar compounds as yet unknown, he would discover them. [...]}}</ref><ref name="PiHKAL">{{CitePiHKAL}} "Mescaline: a magic name and a magic compound. My first encounter with this word was just after World War II, when I returned to Berkeley [...] In the area of serious and thoughtful texts, there were the writings and the famous maps of Alexander Rouhier in 1926. There was the treatise by Kurt Beringer, which described the responses of many scores of subjects to effective doses of mescaline, administered almost always by injection. His book, “Der Meskalinrauche siene Geschichte und Erscheinungsweise,” (1927) has never been translated into English. [...] I read all the more recent literature about it that had appeared, the essays of Aldous Huxley in the mid-1950’s (the exuberant Doors of Perception and the more cautious Heaven and Hell) [...] But it was not until April of 1960 that a psychologist friend of mine, Terry Major, and a friend of his who was studying medicine, Sam Golding, reinforced my interest and provided me with the opportunity to be “babysat” on an experience with 400 milligrams of mescaline sulfate. It was a day that will remain blazingly vivid in my memory, and one which unquestionably confirmed the entire direction of my life. [...]"</ref><ref name="Romero1995" /> A [[psychologist]] friend of Shulgin's named Terry Major offered to let him try mescaline and he eagerly accepted.<ref name="Jay2019" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /> Shulgin's first experience with the drug, at a dose of 350 or 400{{nbsp}}mg of the [[sulfate]] [[salt (chemistry)|salt]], was on April 2, 1960.<ref name="Jay2019" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="Erowid-Peyote-Timeline">{{cite web | title=Erowid Peyote Vault : Timeline | website=www.erowid.org | url=https://www.erowid.org/plants/peyote/peyote_timeline.php | quote=Dr. Alexander Shulgin first tries mescaline at 350 mg. 16, 17   [Details] Notebook 4, page 471 April 2, 1960. 350mg of mescaline administered orally at 9:15A.M. Subjects: A.T. Shulgin, Robert Thompson, Nina Shulgin Observers: Taylor + Veronica Wolf, Henry Brock. There is some confusion around this because he told an LA Times Reporter I first explored mescaline in the late '50s, Shulgin says. Three-hundred-fifty to 400 milligrams. I learned there was a great deal inside me, he replies. However PIHKAL indicates his first mescaline trip was in April 1960 at 400mg, but the hand written notes in Pharmacology Notes IV gives 350mg as the dose. However, a different notebook records a different mescaline trip on April 16, 1960 with just ATS and one observer (DP) where the dose taken was 400mg. We assume that his offhand remark to a reporter about the '50s was just a small memory error and the confusion between 350 and 400mg as his first dose is of no historical importance. [...] 16. Shulgin AT. Pharmacology Notes IV. Page 471. 17. Shulgin AT, Shulgin A. PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story. Transform Press. 1991.}}</ref><ref name="PsychedelicTimes2025">{{cite web | title=Psychedelic Timeline | website=Psychedelic Times | date=2025 | url=https://psychedelictimes.com/psychedelic-timeline/ | quote=1960: April 16th Alexander Shulgin ingested 400mg of mescaline sulfate for the first time. The experience “unquestionably confirmed the entire direction of my life”. He would go on to create over 200 new psychedelic compounds.}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin1981">{{cite book | last = Shulgin | first = Alexander | title = Pharmacology Lab Notes #4 | date = 1981 | pages=471–472 | publisher = Erowid | url = https://erowid.org/library/books_online/shulgin_labbooks/shulgin_pharmacology_notebook4_searchable.pdf#page=32 | quote = April 2, 1960. 350mg of mescaline administered orally at 9:15A.M. Subjects: A.T. Shulgin, Robert Thompson, Nina Shulgin Observers: Taylor + Veronica Wolf, Henry Brock. [...]}}</ref> Speaking of the experience, Shulgin said "I learned there was a great deal inside me".<ref name="Romero1995" /><ref name="Erowid-Peyote-Timeline" /> In addition, he said that the experience "unquestionably confirmed the entire direction of my life".<ref name="Jay2019" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /> Shulgin described experiencing color and visual changes, insights, recall of childhood memories, and experiencing the world as amazing like when he was a child again.<ref name="Jay2019" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /> He later reported personal revelations that "had been brought about by a fraction of a gram of a white solid, but that in no way whatsoever could it be argued that these memories had been contained within the white solid ... I understood that our entire universe is contained in the mind and the spirit. We may choose not to find access to it, we may even deny its existence, but it is indeed there inside us, and there are chemicals that can catalyze its availability."<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /> With the experience, Shulgin decided to study psychedelic drugs and their chemistry and began publishing in this area in early 1961.<ref name="Jay2019" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="Shulgin1961">{{cite journal | last1=Shulgin | first1=Alexander T. | last2=Bunnell | first2=Sterling | last3=Sargent | first3=Thornton | title=The Psychotomimetic Properties of 3,4,5-Trimethoxyamphetamine | journal=Nature | volume=189 | issue=4769 | date=1961 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/1891011a0 | pages=1011–1012 | bibcode=1961Natur.189.1011S | url = https://bibliography.maps.org/resources/download/9105 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250712205552/https://bibliography.maps.org/resources/download/9105 | archive-date=2025-07-12}}</ref>

[[File:Zectran 2009 hanna jon.JPG|thumb|upright|[[Mexacarbate]] (Zectran)-containing pesticide manufactured by Dow; photo taken at the Farm in 2009.]]

Shulgin's professional activities continued to lean in the direction of [[psychopharmacology]], furthered by his personal experiences with psychedelics. But during this period he was unable to do much independent research. His opportunity for further research came in 1961 after his development of [[mexacarbate]] (brand name Zectran), the first [[biodegradable]] pesticide and a highly profitable product.<ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Peplow2014" /><ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014" /> In his book ''[[PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story]]'', Shulgin limits his pesticide days at Dow Chemical to one sentence of the almost 1,000{{nbsp}}pages.<ref name="PiHKAL" /> Dow Chemical Company, in return for mexacarbate's valuable patent, gave Shulgin great freedom.<ref name="Peplow2014" /><ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014" /> During this time, he created and patented drugs when Dow asked, and published findings on other drugs in journals such as ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' and the ''[[Journal of Organic Chemistry]]''.

Shulgin discovered the psychedelic drug [[DOM (drug)|DOM]], which has around 100{{nbsp}}times the [[potency (pharmacology)|potency]] of [[mescaline]], while working at Dow Chemical Company in 1963.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> This led to a research program on DOM and its [[structural analog|analogue]] [[DOET (drug)|DOET]] at the company in the mid-1960s, including clinical studies of DOET for potential medical use at sub-hallucinogenic doses as a "[[psychic energizer]]".<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> They tasked neuroscientist [[Solomon H. Snyder]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]] with conducting the studies.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> Soon after [[LSD]] was banned in California in October 1966, LSD chemist [[Owsley Stanley]] began looking for a legal replacement for it.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> Shulgin provided Stanley with information about DOM's synthesis on index cards and a 50{{nbsp}}g sample of the drug.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> Stanley then began distributing DOM to the public in very-high-dose tablets under the nickname STP in the [[Haight-Ashbury]] district of [[San Francisco]] starting in April 1967.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> This resulted in a small [[public health crisis]] due to unintentional [[overdose]]s, the drug's potential for very long [[duration of action|duration]]s, and its greater [[adverse effect]]s compared to LSD.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> It was soon uncovered and published in the news media that DOM had originated at Dow Chemical Company.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> As a result, the company cancelled its research program into DOET.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /><ref name="Baggott2023" /> In addition, at some point, Dow Chemical Company requested that Shulgin no longer use their name as an affiliation on his publications.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Wolfson2014" />

In December 1966, shortly before the DOM epidemic, Shulgin left Dow Chemical company in order to pursue his own interests.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" /> He first spent two years in [[medical school]] studying [[neurology]] at the [[UCSF School of Medicine|University of California, San Francisco, School of Medicine]],<ref name="Platoni2002" /> leaving to work on a consulting project. Shulgin set up a home-based lab on his property, known as "the Farm" (later called the Shulgin Farm), and became a private consultant. He also taught classes at local universities including the [[University of California, Berkeley]], the [[University of California, San Francisco]], and [[San Francisco State University]].<ref name="Hanna2014" /><ref name="Greendyk2021" /> Through his friend Bob Sager, head of the U.S. [[Drug Enforcement Administration]] (DEA)'s Western Laboratories, Shulgin formed a relationship with the DEA and began holding [[pharmacology]] seminars for the agents, supplying the DEA with samples of various compounds, and occasionally serving as an expert witness in court.<ref name="Wolfson2014" /> In 1988, he authored a then-definitive law enforcement reference book on controlled substances called ''The Controlled Substances Act: A Resource Manual of the Current Status of the Federal Drug Laws''.<ref name="Wolfson2014" /><ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014" /><ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Shulgin1988">{{cite book | vauthors = Shulgin AT | title = The Controlled Substances Act: A Resource Manual of the Current Status of the Federal Drug Laws | edition = 1 | date = 1988 | publisher = A. T. Shulgin | location = Lafayette, California | oclc = 22676094 | ol = OL58242586M | url = https://bibliography.maps.org/bibliography/default/citation/5573}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin1992">{{cite book | vauthors = Shulgin AT | title = Controlled Substances: A Chemical and Legal Guide to the Federal Drug Laws | edition = 2 | date = 1992 | publisher = Ronin Publishing | location = Berkeley, California | isbn = 9780914171430 | oclc = 26815633 | ol = OL1140749M | url = https://archive.org/details/controlledsubsta0000shul}}</ref> He also served as an expert witness for the DEA and received several awards from them.<ref name="Wolfson2014" /><ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014" />

Shulgin developed [[Ariadne (drug)|Ariadne]] (4C-D; BL-3912), a non-hallucinogenic analogue of DOM, in 1968.<ref name="CunninghamBockSerrano2023">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cunningham MJ, Bock HA, Serrano IC, Bechand B, Vidyadhara DJ, Bonniwell EM, Lankri D, Duggan P, Nazarova AL, Cao AB, Calkins MM, Khirsariya P, Hwu C, Katritch V, Chandra SS, McCorvy JD, Sames D | title = Pharmacological Mechanism of the Non-hallucinogenic 5-HT<sub>2A</sub> Agonist Ariadne and Analogs | journal = ACS Chemical Neuroscience | volume = 14 | issue = 1 | pages = 119–135 | date = January 2023 | pmid = 36521179 | pmc = 10147382 | doi = 10.1021/acschemneuro.2c00597 }}</ref><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="ShulginManningDaley2011-Ariadne">{{cite book | vauthors = Shulgin A, Manning T, Daley PF | chapter = #7. ARIADNE | title = [[The Shulgin Index, Volume One: Psychedelic Phenethylamines and Related Compounds]] | location = Berkeley, CA | volume = 1 | pages = 7–9 | year = 2011 | chapter-url = https://archive.org/details/shulgin-index-vol-1/page/7/mode/1up | publisher = Transform Press | isbn = 978-0-9630096-3-0 | oclc = 709667010 | quote = It was developed commercially by the Bristol-Myers Company to increase mental alertness in geriatric patients, and was patented in Germany, France, and the United States (Shulgin, 1974a, 1974b, 1977a). Its commercial name, Dimoxamine, does not have a classic female ring to it. [...] In normal human subjects, R-4C-DOM orally at 25—50 mg increased mental alertness and feelings of well-being. At 100 mg/day, the symptoms of Parkinson's disease went into remission. With psychotic patients there was a consistent relief of manic depression at doses of 50-100 mg (Shulgin, 1977a; Partyka et al., 1978). A single human oral ingestion of 270 mg produced a change of state of consciousness but evoked no psychedelic effects (Winter, 1980).}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin1987">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shulgin AT | title = The "Social-Chemistry" of Pharmacological Discovery: Interview with Dr. Alexander T. Shulgin. January 26, 1986 | journal = Social Pharmacology | volume = 1 | issue = 3 | pages = 279–290 | date = 1987 | url = https://bibliography.maps.org/resources/download/9052 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20250712234907/https://bibliography.maps.org/resources/download/9052 | archive-date = 12 July 2025 }}</ref> Though Ariadne was not psychedelic, it was still psychoactive, producing feelings of well-being and mental alertness analogously to sub-hallucinogenic doses of DOM and DOET.<ref name="CunninghamBockSerrano2023" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="ShulginManningDaley2011-Ariadne" /><ref name="Shulgin1987" /> Shulgin introduced Ariadne to [[Bristol-Myers Company]], which started clinical trials of the drug for various uses in 1974.<ref name="CunninghamBockSerrano2023" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="ShulginManningDaley2011-Ariadne" /><ref name="Shulgin1987" /> It reached [[Phases of clinical research#Phase III|phase 3]] trials and had the tentative brand name Dimoxamine, but development was ultimately discontinued for strategic economic reasons.<ref name="CunninghamBockSerrano2023" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="ShulginManningDaley2011-Ariadne" /><ref name="Shulgin1987" />

==Independent research==
In order to work with scheduled psychoactive chemicals, Shulgin obtained a DEA [[Controlled Substances Act|Schedule I]] license for an [[analytical chemistry|analytical]] laboratory, which allowed him to synthesize and possess any otherwise illicit drug.<ref name="Wolfson2014" /><ref name="Johnson2018">{{Cite book |last=Johnson |first=Cody |title=Magic Medicine: A Trip Through the Intoxicating History and Modern-Day Use of Psychedelic Plants & Substances |date=2018 |isbn=978-1-59233-772-9 |location=Beverly, MA |pages=26 |oclc=1029780854}}</ref> Shulgin set up a [[chemical synthesis]] laboratory in a small building behind his house, which gave him a great deal of career autonomy. Shulgin used this freedom to synthesize and test the effects of potentially [[psychoactive drug]]s.

In 1976, Shulgin was reintroduced to [[MDMA]] by a student in the [[medicinal chemistry]] group he advised at [[San Francisco State University]].<ref name="Brown2002">{{cite magazine|last1=Brown|first1=Ethan|title=Professor X|url=https://www.wired.com/2002/09/professorx/ |magazine=Wired |access-date=January 4, 2015|date=September 1, 2002|archive-date=June 25, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150625015832/http://archive.wired.com/wired/archive/10.09/professorx.html?pg=3&topic=&topic_set=|url-status=live}}</ref> MDMA had been synthesized in 1912 by [[Merck KGaA|Merck]] and patented in 1913 as an intermediate of another synthesis in order to block competitors, but was never explored in its own right. Shulgin went on to develop a new synthesis method, and in 1976, introduced the chemical to [[Leo Zeff]], a [[psychologist]] from [[Oakland, California]]. Zeff used the substance in his practice in small doses as an aid to [[talk therapy]]. Zeff introduced the substance to hundreds of psychologists and lay therapists around the nation, including [[Ann Shulgin|Ann Gotlieb]], whom Alexander Shulgin met in 1979 and married in 1981.<ref name="Bennett2005" /> It was her fourth marriage, and she had four children.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.shulginresearch.org/home/about/ann_shulgin/ |title=Ann Shulgin |website=Shulginresearch.org |access-date=May 11, 2016 |archive-date=May 14, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160514044955/http://www.shulginresearch.org/home/about/ann_shulgin/ |url-status=live }} Detailed biography of Ann Shulgin</ref>

[[File:Shulgin research group circa 1980.jpg|thumb|left|300px|Most of the Shulgin research group circa 1980.<ref name="Simone2016" /> From left to right, [[Darrell Lemaire]], unknown, [[Myron Stolaroff]], Dale, Phyllis, Alexander Shulgin, [[Ann Shulgin]], and [[Peyton Jacob III]].<ref name="Simone2016" />]]

After judicious self-experiments, Shulgin enlisted a small group of friends with whom he regularly tested his creations, starting in 1960. Among these friends included [[Peyton Jacob III]], [[Myron Stolaroff]], Jean Stolaroff, and [[Darrell Lemaire]], among others.<ref name="Simone2016">{{cite journal | last = Simone | first = S. | title = Faces & Places: Sorting Photos in the Shulgin Archive | journal = Erowid Extracts | date = February 2016 | issue = 28 | page = 2 | url = https://erowid.org/culture/characters/shulgin_alexander/shulgin_alexander_article4.shtml}}</ref><ref name="BLTC2021">{{cite AV media | people=Connie Littlefield (director, writer), Siobhan Flanagan, [[Alexander Shulgin]] (subject), [[Ann Shulgin]] (subject), Paul F. Daley (subject), [[Myron Stolaroff]] (subject), Jean Stolaroff (subject), Wendy Perry Tucker (subject), Tania Manning (subject), Greg Manning (subject), [[Keeper Trout]] (subject), [[Erowid|Earth and Fire Erowid]], others | date=2021 | title=Better Living Through Chemistry | url=https://betterlivingthroughchemistry.org/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921000000/https://betterlivingthroughchemistry.org/ | archive-date=21 September 2021 | type=Motion picture | language=English | location= | publisher=Better Living Through Film, Incorporated}} [https://tubitv.com/movies/100015889/better-living-through-chemistry Alt URL]</ref><ref name="PassieBrandt2018" /> Shulgin developed a systematic way of ranking the effects of the various drugs, known as the [[Shulgin Rating Scale]], with a vocabulary to describe the visual, auditory and physical sensations. He personally tested hundreds of drugs, mainly analogues of various [[substituted phenethylamine|phenethylamine]]s (family containing [[ecstasy (drug)|MDMA]], [[mescaline]], [[2C family|2C]]s, and the [[DOx (psychedelics)|DOx]]), and [[substituted tryptamine|tryptamine]]s (family containing [[dimethyltryptamine|DMT]], [[psilocin]], and [[LSD]]). There are a seemingly infinite number of slight chemical variations, which can produce variations in effect—some pleasant and some unpleasant, depending on the person, substance, and situation—all of which are meticulously recorded in Shulgin's laboratory notebooks. Shulgin published many of these objective and subjective reports in his books and papers.<ref name="Bennett2005" /> About [[2C-B]] he said in 2003: "It is, in my opinion, one of the most graceful, erotic, sensual, introspective compounds I have ever invented. For most people, it is a short-lived and comfortable psychedelic, with neither toxic side-effects nor next-day hang-over."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ask Dr. Alexander "Sasha" Shulgin Online – 2C-B |url=https://www.cognitiveliberty.org/ccle1/shulgin/adsarchive/2cb.htm |access-date=July 4, 2022 |website=www.cognitiveliberty.org}}</ref>

With his wife Ann, Shulgin published the books ''[[PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story]]'' (''Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved'') in 1991 and ''[[TiHKAL: The Continuation]]'' (''Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved'') in 1997.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="PassieBrandt2018" /><ref name="Risen2022"/><ref name="Warren2022"/><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="TiHKAL">{{CiteTiHKAL}}</ref> These books documented his and others' work with hundreds of [[substituted phenethylamine|phenethylamine]]s, [[substituted tryptamine|tryptamine]]s, and [[substituted lysergamide|lysergamide]]s, including their [[chemical synthesis|chemical syntheses]], properties and effects, and discussion.<ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="PiHKAL" /><ref name="TiHKAL" /> The Shulgins started their own publishing company, [[Transform Press]], to publish the books.<ref name="Presti2022" />

In 1994, two years after the publication of ''PiHKAL'', the DEA raided his lab. The agency requested that Shulgin surrender his license for violating its terms, and he was fined $25,000 for possession of anonymous samples sent to him for quality testing. In the 15 years preceding the publication of ''PiHKAL'', two announced and scheduled reviews failed to find any irregularities.<ref name="Erowid2004">{{cite web | title = DEA Raid of Shulgin's Laboratory | publisher = [[Erowid]] | date = January 8, 2004 | url = http://www.erowid.org/culture/characters/shulgin_alexander/shulgin_alexander_raid.shtml | access-date = July 8, 2006 | archive-date = March 26, 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070326003950/http://www.erowid.org/culture/characters/shulgin_alexander/shulgin_alexander_raid.shtml | url-status = live }}</ref> Richard Meyer, spokesman for DEA's San Francisco Field Division, has stated that, "It is our opinion that those books are pretty much cookbooks on how to make illegal drugs. Agents tell me that in clandestine labs that they have raided, they have found copies of those books."<ref name="Bennett2005" />

[[File:Shulgin alexander 2009 hanna jon.jpg|thumb|right|275px|Shulgin at the home-based lab on his property, known as "the Farm", 2009. He is wearing an [[Erowid]] shirt.]]

In the 2000s, Shulgin had been working on a series of ''N''-[[allyl group|allylated]] [[substituted tryptamine|tryptamine]]s including [[DALT (drug)|DALT]], [[5-MeO-DALT]], and [[5-MeO-MALT]].<ref name="Morris2010" /><ref name="Shulgin2004a">{{cite web | vauthors = Shulgin AT, Shulgin A | title = DALT | date = 2004 | work = Entry from a Forthcoming Book | url = https://isomerdesign.com/pihkal/read/tk/57}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin2004b">{{cite web | vauthors = Shulgin AT, Shulgin A | title = 5-MeO-DALT | date = August 2004 | work = Entry from a Forthcoming Book | url = https://www.erowid.org/chemicals/5meo_dalt/5meo_dalt_info1.shtml | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20250707213422/https://www.erowid.org/chemicals/5meo_dalt/5meo_dalt_info1.shtml | archive-date = 7 July 2025 | access-date = 7 July 2025 | url-status = bot: unknown }}</ref> He had also been working in the 2000s to identify the active constituents of ''[[Pachycereus pringlei]]'' (cardón or elephant cactus), a [[psychedelic cactus]] native to northwestern [[Mexico]] that does not contain [[mescaline]], though these efforts were ultimately unsuccessful.<ref name="Brown2002" /><ref name="Shulgin2002a">{{cite conference | author = Alexander Shulgin | title = Cacti: A Discourse by Sasha Shulgin | conference = Mind States: Jamaica, October 1–6, 2002 | time = 16:28–17:55, 25:45–28:44, [...] | url = https://archive.org/details/PsychedelicSalon025-sashashulgin-cacti}}</ref><ref name="Telegraph2022">{{cite web | author=Telegraph Obituaries | title=Ann Shulgin, pioneering researcher who with her husband Alexander explored the uses of psychedelic drugs – obituary | website=The Telegraph | date=15 July 2022 | url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2022/07/15/ann-shulgin-pioneering-researcher-who-husband-alexander-explored/ | access-date=20 May 2025 | quote=By no means all Ann and Sasha's experiences with psychedelics were happy ones. In 2001 they tested the cactus Pachycereus pringlei, native to northwestern Mexico, dissolving an extract in fruit juice and each drinking a 100 ml cup. While Sasha was overcome by a fear of movement, Ann "could see the full moon shining down on me with what felt like chilling contempt". This would be, she reflected, "an awful, stupid way to die".}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin2002b">{{cite web | title=Future Psychedelics | website=Ask Dr. Shulgin Online | date=12 June 2002 | url=https://www.cognitiveliberty.org/ccle1/shulgin/adsarchive/future_psychedelic.htm | access-date=20 May 2025}}</ref><ref name="CrockettShulgin2005">{{cite conference | author1 = Earl Crockett | author2 = Alexander Shulgin | title = A New Elixir | conference = Sacred Elixir Conference, San Jose, California on October 22–24, 2005 | date = October 2005 | url = http://www.plantconsciousness.com/a_new_elixir_desc.htm | quote = Earl Crockett has not only discovered that the cactus Pachycereus pringlei has psychedelic properties, he has also discovered cave paintings which reveal its ancient use as a sacrament. His talk describing the discovery of this remarkable plant will be accompanied by slides of the cactus and of the cave paintings. Dr. Shulgin will describe the processes of gas chromatography and mass spectroscopy, how one goes about determining what alkaloids are in a plant and what he found to be present in this cactus. | access-date = 2025-05-20 | archive-date = 2008-11-20 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081120183212/http://www.plantconsciousness.com/a_new_elixir_desc.htm | url-status = bot: unknown }}</ref><ref name="Trout2013">{{cite book | author = [[Keeper Trout & friends]] | title = Cactus Chemistry By Species (Sacred Cacti 4th edition Part C Cactus Chemistry: Section 2) | date = 2014 | publisher = Mydriatic Productions/Better Days Publishing | url = https://troutsnotes.com/pdf/CactusChemistry_2013_Light.pdf#page=55}}</ref> He published the book ''[[The Simple Plant Isoquinolines]]'' in 2003.<ref name="SumnallEvans-BrownMcVeigh2011" /><ref name="Clark2008">{{cite web | last=Clark | first=Jaysen M. | title=The San Pedro Long Dance: Transpersonal aspects of a contemporary entheogenic ritual | date=2008 | website=ProQuest | url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/20d69f130d7194466d4cd6f504ce0db6/1?cbl=18750&pq-origsite=gscholar | access-date=21 May 2025 | quote = For those interested in the chemistry of San Pedro, Shulgin and Perry’s recent publication The Simple Plant Isoquinolines (2002) was an attempt at both sorting through the complex taxonomy of several different cacti and isolating the various chemical constituents within them..}}</ref><ref name="ShulginPerry2002">{{cite book | last=Shulgin | first=Alexander Theodore | last2=Perry | first2=Wendy E. | title=The Simple Plant Isoquinolines | publisher=[[Transform Press]] | date=2002 | isbn=978-0-9630096-2-3 | oclc=51006569 | ol=OL8521520M | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NogvAQAAIAAJ}}</ref> Shulgin ran a web column called Ask Dr. Shulgin Online through the Center for Cognitive Liberty & Ethics (CCLE) from 2001 to 2005.<ref name="AskDrShulginOnline">{{cite web | title=Ask Dr. Shulgin Online | website=cognitiveliberty.org | date=19 September 2019 | url=https://www.cognitiveliberty.org/about-ask-dr-shulgin-online/}}</ref> His final book published during his life, ''[[The Shulgin Index, Volume One: Psychedelic Phenethylamines and Related Compounds]]'', was published in 2011.<ref name="SumnallEvans-BrownMcVeigh2011">{{cite journal | vauthors = Sumnall HR, Evans-Brown M, McVeigh J | title = Social, policy, and public health perspectives on new psychoactive substances | journal = Drug Test Anal | volume = 3 | issue = 7–8 | pages = 515–523 | date = 2011 | pmid = 21744515 | doi = 10.1002/dta.310 | url = | quote = Shulgin's PIHKAL[25] and TIHKAL[26] describe synthesis routes and basic human psychopharmacology of many potential hallucinogenic and entactogenic compounds [...] The Shulgin Index Volume 1, Psychedelic Phenethylamines and Related Compounds (to be followed by a similar volume on tryptamines) was published in 2011,[119] providing a focused, fully referenced examination of the chemistry and pharmacology of 126 compounds, many of them new.}}</ref><ref name="FrancisSmith2022">{{cite book | last1=Francis | first1=Arie P. | last2=Smith | first2=Silas W. | title=Novel Psychoactive Substances | chapter=Availability and supply of novel psychoactive substances | publisher=Elsevier | year=2022 | isbn=978-0-12-818788-3 | doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-818788-3.00001-2 | pages=57–84 | quote=[Novel psychoactive substance (NPS)] development and manufacturing efforts are aided by those with scientific training who develop or scan research literature for novel structures or derivatives [59]. Substituted phenethylamines and tryptamines were explicitly described in the 1990s by synthetic chemist Alexander Shulgin in the books PiHKAL and TiHKAL, which maintain an online presence [101,102]. The Shulgin Index, cataloguing psychedelic phenethylamines, amphetamines, phenylpiperazines, and others, including synthesis and pharmacological properties, was released in 2011 [103].}}</ref><ref name="ShulginManningDaley2011">{{cite book | last1=Shulgin | first1=A. | last2=Manning | first2=T. | last3=Daley | first3=P.F. | title=[[The Shulgin Index, Volume One: Psychedelic Phenethylamines and Related Compounds]] | publisher=[[Transform Press]] | location=Berkeley | volume=1 | year=2011 | isbn=978-0-9630096-3-0}}</ref> A second volume on tryptamines was also being prepared but was ultimately never completed.<ref name="SumnallEvans-BrownMcVeigh2011" /><ref name="Weber2014">{{cite web | last=Weber | first=Bruce | title=Alexander Shulgin, Psychedelia Researcher, Dies at 88 | website=The New York Times | date=7 June 2014 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/06/08/us/alexander-shulgin-psychedelia-researcher-dies-at-88.html | access-date=3 November 2024}}</ref><ref name="MAPS2014b">{{cite journal | author = Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies | title = In Memoriam: Alexander "Sasha" Shulgin, Ph.D. (June 17, 1925–June 2, 2014) | date = Summer 2014 | journal = MAPS Newsletter | volume = 24 | issue = 2 | pages = 9–12 (11) | url = https://maps.org/news-letters/v24n2/v24n2_p9-12.pdf | quote = ON JUNE 2, 2014, AT THE age of 88, pioneering psychedelic researcher Alexander "Sasha" Shulgin died surrounded by friends and family at his home in Lafayette, California. [...] In 2011, his life's work was published in The Shulgin Index, Volume 1: Psychedelic Phenethylamines and Related Compounds. While the first volume contains over 1,300 compounds, there is more to come. The Shulgin Index, Volume 2 will be published in the near future. Sasha understood that the exploration of novel psychoactive compounds—and ways to use them—would not be completed in his lifetime, so he preserved his research in these volumes for future generations.}}</ref> His book ''The Nature of Drugs: History, Pharmacology, and Social Impact'', based on his lectures for a pharmacology course he taught at San Francisco State University in the late 1980s, was published posthumously in two volumes in 2021 and 2023.<ref name="Greendyk2021">{{cite web | last=Greendyk | first=Ryan | title=On Drugs, Freedom, and Human Nature: A Course with Alexander Shulgin | website=Lucid News - Psychedelics | date=17 August 2021 | url=https://www.lucid.news/on-drugs-freedom-and-human-nature-a-course-with-alexander-shulgin/ | access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="Stone2021">{{cite web | last=Stone | first=Katie | title=Grandparents of Psychedelics Ann and Sasha Shulgin Honored by Friends and Fellow Researchers | website=Lucid News - Psychedelics | date=26 July 2021 | url=https://www.lucid.news/grandparents-of-psychedelics-ann-and-sasha-shulgin-honored-by-friends-and-fellow-researchers/ | access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="PsychedelicsToday2021">{{cite web | author=Psychedelic Today | title=Book Review: Alexander Shulgin's The Nature of Drugs | website=Psychedelics Today | date=23 June 2021 | url=https://psychedelicstoday.com/2021/06/23/book-review-alexander-shulgin-the-nature-of-drugs/ | access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin2021">{{cite book | last=Shulgin | first=Alexander | title=The Nature of Drugs: History, Pharmacology, and Social Impact, Volume One | volume = 1 | publisher=[[Transform Press]] | date=2021 | oclc = 1202745911 | isbn=978-0-9995472-1-2 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8DuXzQEACAAJ}}</ref><ref name="Shulgin2023">{{cite book | last=Shulgin | first=Alexander | title=The Nature of Drugs: History, Pharmacology, and Social Impact, Volume Two | volume = 2 | publisher=[[Transform Press]] | date=2023 | oclc = 1388539720 | isbn=9780999547250 | url=https://synergeticpress.com/catalog/the-nature-of-drugs-history-pharmacology-and-social-impact-volume-2/}}</ref>

==Personal life, health, and death==
Shulgin was married to Nina Shulgin (née Gordon) until her death from a [[stroke]] in 1977.<ref name="Vastag2014">{{cite news | last=Vastag | first=Brian | title=Chemist Alexander Shulgin, popularizer of the drug Ecstasy, dies at 88 | newspaper=Washington Post | date=3 June 2014 | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/chemist-alexander-shulgin-popularizer-of-the-drug-ecstasy-dies-at-88/2014/06/03/19fd9580-eb34-11e3-b98c-72cef4a00499_story.html | access-date=2 November 2024}}</ref><ref name="Hanna2014">{{cite web | last=Hanna | first=Jon | title=Alexander Theodore Shulgin (1925–2014) | website=openDemocracy | date=9 June 2014 | url=https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/alexander-theodore-shulgin-19252014/ | access-date=2 November 2024}}</ref> He had a son with her, Theodore "Ted" Shulgin.<ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Sauret2010" /> Following Nina's death, Shulgin married [[Ann Shulgin]] (née Gotlieb) in 1981.<ref name="Weber2014" /><ref name="Hanna2014" /> He spent most of his later life at the Farm in [[Lafayette, California]]. Shulgin's son Ted died in 2011 at the age of 61.<ref name="Power2014" /><ref name="Vastag2014" /> Ted had helped Shulgin in [[chemical synthesis|synthesizing]] [[DOM (drug)|DOM]] as a teenager in 1963.<ref name="TroutDaley2024" />

On April 8, 2008, at the age of 82, Shulgin underwent surgery to replace a defective [[aortic valve]].<ref name="MAPS2008">{{cite journal|title=MAPS News: June 2008 – First legal dose of LSD administered! |url=http://www.maps.org/sys/nq.pl?id=1610 |date=June 19, 2008 |journal=MAPS News |author =Brown, David Jay |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120302181622/http://www.maps.org/sys/nq.pl?id=1610 |archive-date=March 2, 2012 }}</ref> He is said to have been almost [[blindness|blind]] in 2010.<ref name="Martin2010">{{cite web | last=Martin | first=Michael | title=Love and Other Drugs | website=Interview Magazine | date=20 August 2010 | url=https://www.interviewmagazine.com/culture/love-and-other-drugs | access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref> On November 16, 2010, Shulgin suffered a stroke, from which he largely recovered.<ref name="Power2010">{{cite web | last=Power | first=Mike | title='Godfather of ecstasy' Alexander Shulgin suffers stroke | website=The Guardian | date=23 November 2010 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2010/nov/23/godfather-ecstasy-alexander-shulgin-stroke | access-date=18 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="Baggott2010">{{cite web|title=Sasha Shulgin |work=Psychedelic Research |date=November 18, 2010 |url=http://psychedelicresearch.org/?p=125 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150222021100/http://psychedelicresearch.org/?p=125 |archive-date=February 22, 2015 }}</ref> Also at the close of 2010, a [[skin-grafting]] surgery saved his left foot from being [[amputation|amputated]]. Around this time, Shulgin began showing early signs of [[dementia]], mostly severe [[memory impairment|loss of short-term memory]]. With progression of the dementia since 2010, his wife, Ann Shulgin, had been trying to sell part of their property to raise more money to cover care costs. On April 17, 2014, Ann Shulgin reported on Facebook that her husband had developed [[liver cancer]], and in a May 31 update on Facebook she said that, although appearing frail, he seemed to be experiencing his last moments in peace and without pain.<ref>{{cite web |author=Pescovitz, David |url=http://boingboing.net/2014/06/01/psychedelic-hero-alexander-shu.html |title=Psychedelic hero Alexander Shulgin nearing death / Boing Boing |publisher=Boingboing.net |date=June 1, 2014 |access-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117222821/http://boingboing.net/2014/06/01/psychedelic-hero-alexander-shu.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Shulgin died at his home on June 2, 2014, at the age of 88.<ref name="Calamur2014" />

Shulgin is said to have had more than 4,000 [[psychedelic experience]]s during his life.<ref name="Risen2022" /><ref name="Kent2022" /> His favorite [[psychedelic drug]] is said to have been [[LSD]],<ref name="Kent2022" /> while his favorite psychedelic of his own creations was [[2C-B]].<ref name="Morris2010" /><ref name="Biello2008">{{cite web | last=Biello | first=David | title=Self-Experimenters: Psychedelic Chemist Explores the Surreality of Inner Space, One Drug at a Time | website=Scientific American | date=20 March 2008 | url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/self-experimenter-chemist-explores-new-psychedelics/ | access-date=11 February 2026 | quote=His personal favorite, which he describes as "extraordinarily comfortable and quite erotic," is known simply as 2C-B for its chemical makeup.}}</ref><ref name="Kent2014" /><ref name="Kent2022" /> When asked what his favorite [[psychoactive drug]] in general was, he responded "probably a nice, moderately expensive [[Zinfandel]]" (a type of [[red wine]]).<ref name="Vastag2014" /> Shulgin personally disliked [[cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] and [[ketamine]], as he didn't like feeling that [[disorientation|disoriented]] and as he valued drugs that provided learning experiences, which he felt that these substances didn't provide in his case.<ref name="Kent2022">{{cite web | last=Kent | first=James | title=Remembering Psychedelic Chemist Alexander Shulgin | website=Psychedelic Spotlight | date=17 June 2022 | url=https://psychedelicspotlight.com/remembering-psychedelic-chemist-alexander-shulgin/ | access-date=11 February 2026 | quote=Although Shulgin never met a psychoactive plant he wouldn’t explore, he was not fond of smoking marijuana. “He didn’t really get along with pot,” says Ann, who shared a similar dislike of the experience. “He just thought, you know, what’s the point of sitting around being stoned all the time. He didn’t think there was much to be learned from the experience.” He had a similar feeling about the dissociative hallucinogen Ketamine. “He really didn’t like being that disoriented,” says Ann. “He was always looking to learn something from the experience. He was looking for a teacher to show him something.” Shulgin’s favorite drug was LSD, [...] When I ask Ann what Sasha’s favorite of his own chemicals is she knows immediately. “It would have to be 2C-B. He was always very proud of that one. He called it the Great Teacher. Although I preferred 2C-B-Fly a bit more.” But there are so many to choose from. DiPT, 5-MeO-AMT, 5-MeO-DALT, Methylone, 2C-T-7, and this list goes on. Ann can’t say for sure how many trips they shared together, she just smiles and says, “We stopped counting at around two-thousand.” This is a mind-boggling number considering the total may actually be closer to four-thousand.}}</ref> When asked which psychedelic he would recommend for someone who had not previously had a psychedelic experience, Shulgin would often say 2C-B.<ref name="Margolin2022" />

Shulgin was a self-proclaimed and staunch [[libertarian]] in the area of psychoactive drugs, advocating personal freedom and [[cognitive liberty]] with little in the way of restrictions.<ref name="Brown2002" /><ref name="Bennett2005" /><ref name="Oroc2014">{{cite web | last=Oroc | first=James | title=The Second Psychedelic Revolution Part Two: Alexander 'Sasha' Shulgin, The Psychedelic Godfather | website=Reality Sandwich | date=28 February 2014 | url=https://realitysandwich.com/second-psychedelic-revolution-part-two/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140228000000/https://realitysandwich.com/second-psychedelic-revolution-part-two/ | archive-date=28 February 2014 | access-date=31 August 2026}} [https://maps.org/2014/02/28/the-second-psychedelic-revolution-part-two-alexander-sasha-shulgin-the/ Alt URL]</ref> He was a member of [[Mensa International]] and frequently attended Mensa events in California.<ref name="PiHKAL" /> Shulgin was also a [[List of Bohemian Club members|Bohemian Club member]] and described this briefly in his book ''[[PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story]]''.<ref name="Brown2002" /><ref name="MAPS2014a">{{cite web |title=Chemist Alexander Shulgin, Popularizer of the Drug Ecstasy, Dies at 88 |url=https://maps.org/news/media/alexander-shulgin-chemist-behind-mdma-dies-at-88/ |website=MAPS |date=June 3, 2014 |language=en-gb}}</ref><ref name="Morris2010" /><ref name="PiHKAL" />

== Response and legacy ==
{{Expand section|date=July 2026}}

In a 2014 [[Review article|review]] of the [[chemical synthesis|synthesis]] of [[designer drug]]s, the effects of Shulgin's work were described as "by far the most far-reaching" effects associated with the cultural climate of interest at the time in hallucinogenic compounds generally and mescaline in particular, with which various artists and writers had experimented. Shulgin said that mescaline made him aware of a world submerged in human spirit, whose "availability" was "catalyzed" by such chemicals; the consequences of his insights were called "devastating" by the reviewers.<ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014" /> In the same review, an example of his insights was given by his description of MDMA as "his low-calorie Martini".<ref name="AppendinoMinassiTaglialatela-Scafati2014" />
